title: Rav Athi (Ithi), colleague of Rav Ashi
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: This amora has been forgotten like one dead and gone. Wherever Rav Asi was found together with Rav Ashi or Rava, the text was emended and it was said that this was the earlier Rav Ashi.

They went still further and gave this earlier Rav Ashi—who never existed—a son named Mar bar Rav Ashi as well. Thus, Ketubot 8a relates that Rav Asi visited Rav Ashi’s house at the wedding celebration of his son Mar; they said that this meant the earlier Rav Ashi. According to their account, we must suppose that there were three sages named Rav Ashi: one in Rav Huna’s time, who was even greater than Rav Huna, since Shabbat 60b and Avodah Zarah 60a record Rav Huna raising an objection to Rav Ashi; another who was Rava’s student; and a third who was born when Rava died.

But when we examine every place where Rav Asi occurs together with Rav Ashi, the latter is always Rav Ashi, the colleague of Ravina. There was only one Rav Ashi, who was fortunate enough still to receive teachings from Rava. This accords with Rambam’s introduction to the Mishneh Torah, where he states that Rav Ashi received from Rava. The Talmudic passage, cited here as Yoma 38b, is read: “Before Rava died, Rav Ashi was born.”

There were, however, three amoraim named Rav Asi. The first was Rav Asi, the colleague of Rav Kahana. The second was Rav Asi, the colleague of Rabbi Ami, who went up to the Land of Israel. The third was called Rabbi or Rav Asi; he was in the Land of Israel and went down to Babylonia with all the traveling scholars in Rava’s time, when the academies of the Land of Israel were destroyed.

Here is the remarkable point: the real name of this last Rav Asi was Rav Athi or Ithi. Wherever he is mentioned with Rav Ashi, Dikdukei Soferim always gives the reading Rav Athi. As noted in the annotations to Sukkah 8a, the Soncino printing had the correct reading; only in the Venice printing, where this name was unfamiliar, was it changed to Rabbi Asi. This is clear. This Rav Asi sat before Rava. Thus, in Shabbat 95b, Rava stated that there were five measures; Rav Asi said, “I heard,” and Rava replied, “Perhaps what you heard was only,” and so forth. This is the same Rav Asi who was Rav Ashi’s colleague. In Eruvin 39b, too, Rav Asi’s words follow Rava’s as an answer, and there is no need to corrupt the text there. Likewise, in Ketubot 22b Rabbi Asi supplies an answer after Rava. Maharsha aptly writes there: “We find that Rav Asi was a later sage, after Abaye and Rava.” Yefeh Einayim writes similarly on Shabbat 95b. He was Rav Ashi’s colleague and took part with him in arranging the Talmud. Thus, in Sukkah 8a, Mar Kashisha, the son of Rav Chisda, said to Rav Ashi, “Do you suppose that a person occupies one cubit?” Rav Asi—Rav Athi in Dikdukei Soferim—said to Rav Ashi, “Indeed, a person occupies one cubit,” and so forth. This shows explicitly that he spoke with Rav Ashi, who arranged the Talmud. Similarly, Eruvin 64b and Zevachim 6a have Rav Asi—Rav Athi in Dikdukei Soferim—speaking to Rav Ashi, and Avodah Zarah 33b records a disagreement between Rav Asi and Rav Ashi. Bekhorot 36a likewise has their disagreement, with Rav Asi saying to Rav Ashi, “But the school of Menashya taught.” In Shabbat 145b the reading has been corrupted to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, but Dikdukei Soferim preserves the correct reading there too: a disagreement between Rav Ithi and Rav Ashi, with Rav Ithi addressing Rav Ashi. The Soncino printing also has this reading. This is the sage of whom Ketubot 8a says that Rav Asi visited Rav Ashi’s house at the wedding celebration of his son Mar. In Zevachim 99a we find Rav Asi together with Rav Yirmeyah of Difti, Rava’s student. Bava Metzia 90b asks about a person’s young son: R' Achi prohibits, while Rav Ashi permits. This shows that the text originally read Rav Athi, as in Dikdukei Soferim; a copyist unfamiliar with that name changed it to R' Achi. Similarly, where Eruvin 10a has Rav Achi proposing an explanation before Rav Yosef, Dikdukei Soferim reads Rav Athi before Rav Ashi. In Chullin 141b, where Rav Idi addresses Rav Ashi, Dikdukei Soferim reads Rav Athi; so do all the old printings. This Rabbi Asi had a son named Rav Sama, who sat before Rav Ashi, as in Ketubot 33b; he is mentioned in Avodah Zarah 50b as Rav Sama bar Athi according to the reading of Dikdukei Soferim.
The author of Dorot ha-Rishonim has already discussed this at length in volume 2, page 290.

Ahavat Tziyon vi-Yerushalayim, Maaserot, page 122, criticizes Dorot ha-Rishonim and says that his statement was merely a display of ingenuity and empty casuistry. Its author did not know that Rabbi Athi was a late sage of Rav Ashi’s generation.

notes.text: Athi, Ati, and Ithi represent the spellings אתי and איתי. The title distinguishes this later figure from the earlier Rav Asi and from Rabbi Asi, Rabbi Ami’s colleague; Hyman’s Hebrew heading uses Asi.

Rambam’s introduction to Mishneh Torah states that Rav Ashi received the tradition from Rava. The birth formula occurs in Kiddushin 72b as “When Rava died, Rav Ashi was born.” Hyman cites Yoma 38b, which gives the general principle about the succession of righteous people, and reads “Before Rava died.”

The consulted Shabbat 145b text has Rav (Ammi) [Ittai] prohibiting and Rav Asi permitting, followed by Rav Ammi addressing Rav Asi. Hyman reports a different reading, Athi/Ithi and Rav Ashi, from Dikdukei Soferim and Soncino. His readings of those printings and his account of how the names changed are retained as his textual argument.

Compare Hyman’s separate articles on [Rav Asi](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-9022ca7e706930d3&lang=en) and [Rabbi Asi, colleague of Rabbi Ami](https://www.girsology.com/toledot?entry=h-63bc6d04b074b84e&lang=en).
